newsitem.title: USA: Defense wraps up case against Ariz. governor.
newsitem.headline: Defense wraps up case against Ariz. governor.

text.p: John Dowd, lead attorney for Arizona Gov. Fife Symington, put his felony fraud case in the hands of jurors Thursday by asserting his client made mistakes on financial documents as a developer, but committed no crime.
Prosecutors were expected to wrap up their rebuttal Friday. The jury was expected to get the case by the end of the day.

Dowd claimed at the end of the 13-week trial that the "three-month audit" by government prosecutors in U.S. District Court revealed "errors and omissions" that meant virtually nothing and left no victims.
"Making mistakes or a series of mistakes is not a crime; if it is we are all in trouble," Dowd told the jury.
He concluded with the reminder to the panel that the stakes were high in this case -- not just for the two-term governor, but for "every citizen who fills out a financial statement."
The financial statements formed the core of the charges against the state's Republican chief executive.
Symington, 51, faces 19 felony counts linked to what statements he gave to lenders.
The government charged him with defrauding lenders by submitting false financial statements in the mid-1980s to early 1990s to keep his real estate empire from crumbling.
He also faces one count each of attempted extortion and perjury in an indictment issued last summer.
If convicted on a single count, he would be ousted from the office he has held since 1991. He faces prison if found guilty on any of the charges.
During his five-hour summation, Dowd urged the jury to toss aside the "distortions" made by the federal government and see Symington as a developer who did his best as the real estate market crashed.

Dowd downplayed charges that lenders relied on information in Symington's financial statements. He claimed that the various financial institutions gave him money based on his "reputation, track record and development skills."
According to Dowd, Symington fed lenders a steady diet of financial information that he pulled together with good intentions.
He accused Symington's accountants, Coopers & Lybrand, of an "inexcusable failure" in checking financial statements sent to lenders.
Dowd added that allegations that Symington attempted to extort loan concessions from labour unions were "cooked up."
The governor is charged with threatening to use the power of his office to seek relief from the unions that loaned him $10 million for a downtown Phoenix office-retail project.
Dowd also said Symington did not commit perjury during a 1995 bankruptcy hearing because he believed at the time that the financial statement in question was accurate.
